q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) > 4) SELECT DISTINCT ID, NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) > 5) SELECT DISTINCT ID, NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because the HAVING clause in Q1 uses COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) > 4 while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) > 5. This difference in threshold changes the set of students (IDs) included in the result set, making the two queries produce different outputs.
counterexample_dsp: Create a small test database with a single student who takes 5 distinct time slots. Q1 will include this student (since 5 > 4), but Q2 will not (since 5 is not > 5).
